sentences.text: Straight – Hampton Roads was a branch of Straight Inc., the Florida-based adolescent drug program, at the Greenbrier area of Chesapeake, Virginia.
It opened in 1989 and closed on February 11, 1991, weeks after state licensing investigators arrived.
Investigators found that untrained people, including other clients, restrained teenagers who tried to leave, and that one teen's arm had been broken.
After it closed, The Virginian-Pilot found from interviews with former clients, their parents and state licensing officials that "severe tactics were the norm" there.
Before 1989, Hampton Roads families sent their children to Straight's center in Springfield, Virginia.
In May 1989, with about 70 local families in that program, the Daily Press reported that Straight planned to open in Chesapeake that summer.
In its own description to the paper, Straight was a five-phase program lasting about a year.
New clients lived with "host families" whose own child was further along, in homes with alarm systems and locked knives and medicines, and visits from their own families had to be earned.
Treatment cost $11,000 to $12,000 a year.
The method relied on "positive peer pressure," giving older clients growing authority over newcomers.
By February 1991 the Chesapeake center had 58 clients from Hampton Roads and 24 staff, took no state or federal money, and was one of eight Straight centers nationwide.
State regulators had already moved against Straight in Virginia.
In 1990, after Washington-area parents complained about the Springfield center, a court agreement required both Virginia centers to change their restraint and living practices.
Early in 1991 parents' complaints brought a licensing specialist to the Chesapeake center, followed by a six-person team from the Department of Mental Health, Mental Retardation and Substance Abuse.

The licensing bureau found that "unqualified individuals, including clients, were allowed to restrain clients if they decided to leave the program," a practice assistant commissioner Jacqueline Ennis called dangerous; one teen's arm had been broken.
It also told the program to limit how many clients each host home took and to check that the homes were adequate.

A Chesapeake mother told the paper she had pulled her 16-year-old son out of the program after less than a month; in the paper's words, when he tried to run away "several of the other clients threw him on the floor to keep him from leaving," and when he tried again "another client grabbed him by the shirt collar, burning his neck and ripping off the shirt."
"When I found him he was having an asthma attack," she said.
The week before, the bureau had refused to renew the Springfield center's license.

A suit in Chesapeake Circuit Court alleged that a Straight counselor, Ken Barker, kissed and touched a client; Wes Fager's 2002 list of cases against Straight gives its trial date as January 8, 1991, and its outcome as unknown.

sources.cite: Wesley M. Fager, "Some Civil Suits and Criminal Cases Against Straight, Inc. and Straight-descendent programs," May 27, 2002

sentences.text: In early February 1991 the center's administrator, Margaret Allen, announced it would close.
She said investigators were "harassing" the program with unannounced visits, and Ennis answered that the inspections were "the normal course of the job."
The center closed on February 11, and all but two of its 58 clients were moved to other Straight programs.

The Virginian-Pilot reported on March 1 that the center's methods included restraints in which youngsters "were held with their arms and legs pulled behind them and their head pushed to the floor," confrontations so close "that spit flew in their faces," and drug searches "that required new enrollees to squat naked in front of other clients."

A Newport News client who left after six months told the paper, "If you're caught in a lie they stand you up, yell and scream at you. Spit flies in your face. You can't move. They hold your arms so you can't get away. You have to stand there and take it."
The paper reported that he "was made to sit for 12-hour sessions in which he was berated and humiliated."
His mother said, "They did things that, if I had done them, I would have been charged with child abuse."
Straight denied the abuse allegations.
